text: Technical effort is rated Medium because the source provides pre-computed, peer-reviewed climate hazard indices (e.g. Hot Days count, SPI-3 drought index) via the ECDE indicator dataset on the CDS, so no own index or threshold definition is needed, unlike raw Copernicus CDS variables. However, geocoding of exposure addresses and grid extraction are still required, and grid resolution varies by indicator (5km to approximately 28km).

Technical effort is rated Medium because NUTS-aggregated hazard layers are usable directly via API or download, requiring only regional lookup rather than own index definition. However, the finer shapefile/raster layers within the Exposure Analysis and Historical Events modules require geocoding and a spatial overlay before they can be joined to individual exposures.

Technical effort is rated High because the fire danger forecast (~8-16km GeoTIFF, varies daily) and the burnt-area layer (250m/20m, satellite-derived) are two separate raw raster products with no ready-made exposure score. Unlike the Low-rated BWV/HQ30 and WLV vector datasets with predefined hazard zones, both EFFIS layers require own geocoding, index interpretation and GIS overlay, and the institution must define how to collapse the time-varying daily fire danger index into a single static attribute per exposure.

Technical effort is rated High because the source provides raw climate variables (NetCDF/GRIB grid data) without any ready-made risk classification. Every use requires selecting the correct variable(s) and building a bespoke climatological and GIS pipeline, including own index and threshold definition, before a variable becomes an exposure-level attribute. This is comparable to other raw-variable sources and contrasts with the ready-made products under copernicus_climate_indicators.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source is a single national dataset (HQ30/HQ100/HQ300 flood extent family) with its own INSPIRE Atom download service and WMS/WFS endpoints. It requires geocoding of portfolio locations and a standard spatial overlay, but no merging of separate underlying datasets - the same pipeline shape as the WLV Gefahrenzonenplan.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source is a single national shapefile dataset with its own download service. It requires geocoding and a standard spatial overlay, but no merging of separate state datasets, consistent with hq_flood_extent (HQ30), which has near-identical technical characteristics.

The source is based on a statutory hazard assessment under the Forstgesetz, produced by the Forsttechnischer Dienst fuer Wildbach- und Lawinenverbauung (data.gv.at, n.d.-b). Known issues: the design event is an approximately 150-year return period; zones represent process boundaries rather than inundation lines and include erosion and sediment-transport processes, so they are not directly comparable to flood inundation areas such as HQ30/HQ100/HQ300.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source provides ready-made facility-level risk scores, directly integrable via API. No own index definition, geocoding or spatial processing is required beyond sending exposure coordinates or addresses to the API; the result is returned at facility level and can be joined directly to the portfolio.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source provides ready-made facility-level scores via a web tool or API. As with other commercial facility-level providers, no own index definition or spatial processing is required; the result is returned directly at facility level for the queried location.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source is a single CSV file keyed to the Firmenbuchnummer. It joins directly to a loan portfolio without GIS or geocoding work. The assigned OeNACE codes are 5-digit; the 4-digit NACE level required by D 01.01 is obtained by dropping the last digit. No spatial processing or climatological modelling is required.

The source is based on the official OeNACE 2025 (NACE Rev. 2.1) assignment maintained by Statistik Austria under section 21 of the Bundesstatistikgesetz (Statistik Austria, n.d.). This was independently verified through structural analysis of the 682 distinct codes: division 45 is absent (abolished in Rev. 2.1), classes 47.41-47.43 are absent (merged into 47.40), and class 46.89 is present (newly created in Rev. 2.1), confirming alignment with the revision required by Template D 01.01. Known issues: companies without an assigned code remain unmatched, and unregistered sole traders are out of scope.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source provides a ready-made OeNACE 2025 classification per entity, delivered directly via API. No manual extract handling, geocoding or spatial processing is required, consistent with the Low rating for hvd_fbnr_oenace, though access here is per-query rather than bulk-file-based.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source is accessed through a statistics dashboard with no download or API, the same interface type as the EBA ESG Dashboard. The rating reflects only the effort to access and read the ECB's own published methodology and aggregate statistics; the separate, substantially higher effort of replicating the methodology with AnaCredit/JRC/Copernicus-equivalent inputs is a distinct undertaking and is described under Suitability, not folded into this column.

The source combines the downloadable Risk Data Library, comprising various national and global hazard datasets of differing provenance, with ThinkHazard!, a simplified categorical screening tool built on harvested hazard layers (GFDRR, n.d.). Known issues: granularity is not uniform across the source - ThinkHazard! resolves to district (ADM2) level, while individual Risk Data Library datasets vary in format and resolution, for example the global landslide hazard map being a continuous grid rather than administrative-boundary based.

Varies by product: ERA5-HEAT is regularly extended as new ERA5 data become available; SMHI hydrology projections are static 30-year model outputs (not continuously updated).

Technical effort is rated Low because each product (ERA5-HEAT, SMHI hydrology) is a purpose-built, ready-made indicator with documented methodology - peer-reviewed for ERA5-HEAT, produced by a named national institute (SMHI) for the hydrology dataset - so no own index or threshold definition is needed, unlike raw copernicus_cds variables. Only geocoding and grid extraction are required beyond querying the API.

The source is based on two distinct production chains: the fire danger forecast is numerical-weather-model output (ECMWF/MeteoFrance), while the burnt-area database is satellite-derived (MODIS/Sentinel-2) and manually validated by the EFFIS network of national fire experts (JRC/Copernicus EMS, n.d.). Known issues: the burnt-area database has a minimum mapped fire size of 30 hectares, excluding smaller fires, and EFFIS is organisationally distinct from the CEMS Fire Danger historical dataset hosted separately on the CDS, which covers meteorological reconstruction only, not observed fire events.

Climate-ADAPT is a public knowledge portal operated by the European Environment Agency (EEA) (EEA, n.d.-a). It provides pre-computed, peer-reviewed climate hazard indices via the European Climate Data Explorer (ECDE), covering heat, precipitation, flood, drought, storm and wildfire hazards at EU-wide scope and grid-based granularity (0.1-0.25 degrees, 5km for hydrology-based indices) (EEA/C3S, n.d.). The source is accessed through a web portal, a queryable API and direct download, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that heat stress and water stress are only covered via indirect proxies (UTCI; aridity), not dedicated indicators (EEA, 2021). In particular, these two proxies were not designed as hazard-specific indices and require careful interpretation before being treated as equivalent to the source's genuinely dedicated indices for heat wave, flood, drought, storm and wildfire. Consequently, the proxy-based hazards cannot be used with the same confidence as the dedicated ones, unless cross-checked against a hazard-specific source.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is providing ready-made, peer-reviewed hazard indices with documented methodology (EEA/C3S, n.d.), saving the index-definition effort that raw climate variables would require. It is particularly useful as a low-effort screening layer for the hazards it does cover. However, its suitability is reduced by incomplete hazard coverage and grid resolution coarser than Austria's parcel-level sources. It is therefore best used as a supplementary source alongside the dedicated Austrian hazard layers.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then query or download the relevant ECDE indicator dataset (sis-ecde-climate-indicators, hosted on the CDS) and assign the returned indicator value to each exposure. The result is grid-level (5km to approximately 28km, depending on indicator). The process is fully automatable.

The source is available under the same CC-BY 4.0 licence that applies to the underlying Copernicus Climate Data Store since 2 July 2025 (ECMWF Forum, 2025). Attribution is required when the data is reused. The licence permits commercial use and systematic portfolio processing.

The Risk Data Hub (RDH) is a public multi-hazard risk and loss data platform operated by the Joint Research Centre (JRC) in cooperation with the EU Disaster Risk Management Knowledge Centre (DRMKC) (JRC DRMKC, n.d.). It provides modelled hazard, exposure and historical-loss data covering flood, landslide, earthquake, wildfire and subsidence at NUTS 2/3 granularity across EU, EFTA and IPA countries (Antofie et al., 2023). The source is accessed through a web portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that the Vulnerability and Risk Analysis modules are documented by JRC itself as 'ongoing work'. In particular, only the Exposure Analysis and Historical Events modules provide reliably usable, hazard-verified layers at present. Consequently, the source's modelled hazard layers cannot be treated as uniformly mature across all five hazards it addresses, unless cross-checked against the specific module status documented per hazard.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable. Its main advantage is EU-wide consistent methodology combined with genuine hazard-and-exposure modelling for five hazards (Antofie et al., 2023). It is particularly useful for substantive risk determination at data point 0050. However, its suitability is reduced by NUTS 2/3-level granularity, coarser than Austria's parcel-level sources, and by being over-specified for the pure Geography reporting requirement. It is therefore best used as a primary source for hazard determination, complemented by finer Austrian layers where available.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then identify the corresponding NUTS 2/3 region and query or download the relevant hazard module via API or shapefile, assigning the regional value to each exposure. The result is regional (NUTS 2/3), not parcel-level. The process is fully automatable.

The source is available under an open EU data licence with attribution required, consistent with JRC's general data-sharing terms (JRC DRMKC, n.d.). The licence permits commercial use and systematic portfolio processing, provided that the source is appropriately credited.

EFFIS (European Forest Fire Information System) is a public wildfire information service operated jointly by the JRC and the Copernicus Emergency Management Service (JRC/Copernicus EMS, n.d.). It provides a daily fire danger forecast and a historical burnt-area database covering wildfire hazard across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa at grid resolutions ranging from approximately 8-16km (forecast) to 250m/20m (observed burnt area) (EFFIS, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through an OGC map service (WMS/WFS) and direct download, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that the fire danger forecast grid (~8-16km) is coarse relative to Austria's size, covering the whole country with only a handful of grid cells. In particular, the much finer 250m/20m burnt-area layer is retrospective/observational rather than a forward-looking exposure indicator, so it cannot substitute for the coarser forecast when a forward-looking classification is needed. Consequently, the source cannot support fine-grained forward-looking wildfire exposure classification on its own, unless combined with the observed burnt-area history for plausibility checks.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is being the only dedicated European wildfire dataset covering both forecast fire danger and observed fire history (JRC/Copernicus EMS, n.d.). It is particularly useful for national-level wildfire screening and historical plausibility checks. However, its suitability is reduced by the coarse forecast-grid resolution for a country the size of Austria and by the raw, unprocessed nature of both layers. It is therefore best used as a supplementary source for wildfire, complemented by own aggregation of the raw data.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then query the WMS/WFS service or download the relevant GeoTIFF layer (fire danger forecast or burnt area) and extract the raster cell value at each coordinate, assigning it to the exposure. The result is grid-level (~8-16km for fire danger, 250m/20m for burnt area). The process is partly automatable, since aggregating the time-varying raster into a single exposure attribute requires a methodological choice.

The source is available under a CC BY 4.0 licence, as confirmed on EFFIS's own dedicated data-licence page (EFFIS, n.d.-c). Attribution is required when the data is reused. The licence permits commercial use and systematic portfolio processing.

The Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS) is a public climate data repository operated by ECMWF on behalf of the EU (ECMWF, n.d.), comprising over 140 datasets of raw and derived climate variables and reanalysis/projection data. It provides raw climate variables (e.g. temperature, precipitation, wind fields) covering multiple physical hazards at grid resolutions of roughly 0.1-0.25 degrees globally, with an EU focus. The source is accessed through a web portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that the source provides raw climate variables rather than ready-made hazard indicators. In particular, every use requires selecting the correct raw variable(s) and building a bespoke climatological/GIS pipeline, and individual sub-datasets may carry stricter licence terms than the general CC-BY 4.0 (e.g. E-OBS, restricted to non-commercial research/education use). Consequently, the source cannot be used directly for exposure classification, unless the institution builds and validates its own index-derivation methodology.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is being authoritative, EU-wide consistent and covering the broadest range of underlying climate variables of any source in the matrix (ECMWF, n.d.). It is particularly useful as the raw-data foundation when no ready-made indicator exists elsewhere. However, its suitability is reduced by the substantial climatological and GIS processing effort required before any variable becomes an exposure classification. It is therefore best used as a fallback source for hazards not covered by ready-made products, rather than as an operational primary source.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then select and download the relevant climate variable(s) in NetCDF/GRIB format and derive a hazard-relevant indicator through own climatological modelling, assigning the result to each exposure. The result is grid-level (~0.1-0.25 degrees). The process requires substantial manual/methodological intervention and is not fully automatable without an own index-derivation methodology.

The source is available under CC-BY 4.0 since 2 July 2025, replacing the previous bespoke "Licence to Use Copernicus Products" (Version 1.2, Nov 2019) that governed CDS access before that date (ECMWF Forum, 2025). Attribution is required when the data is reused. Individual sub-datasets may carry stricter third-party terms and should be verified per dataset before use.

The EBA ESG Dashboard is a public statistics dashboard operated by the European Banking Authority (EBA) (EBA, n.d.-a). It provides aggregated ESG risk indicators at EU bank level, covering both physical and transition climate risk at institution/portfolio-level granularity across the EU/EEA (EBA, n.d.-a). The source is accessed through a statistics dashboard, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that the source provides only aggregate EU bank-level statistics (EBA, n.d.-a). In particular, no download or API access exists and no per-exposure data is available whatsoever. Consequently, the source cannot be used to populate any individual exposure in D 01.01, unless it is used purely for peer-comparison or benchmarking purposes.

For an SNCI, the source is not suitable for populating individual exposures. Its main advantage is providing an authoritative EU/EEA peer-comparison benchmark (EBA, n.d.-a). It is particularly useful for contextualising an institution's own physical and transition risk exposure against sector averages. However, its suitability is reduced by the complete absence of per-exposure or downloadable data. It is therefore best used purely as a context/benchmarking source, not as an operational data source.
Not applicable: the source provides only aggregate EU bank-level statistics with no per-exposure data (EBA, n.d.-a), so no portfolio-level pipeline can be built against it.

The source is available under the EBA's standard open-data terms, free of charge and without registration (EBA, n.d.-a). No restrictions on commercial or systematic use beyond standard attribution practice were identified.

This is a public methodological and statistical resource operated by the European Central Bank (ECB) (ECB, n.d.). It provides a documented physical-risk indicator methodology and euro-area aggregate statistics, covering coastal flooding, river flooding, wildfires, landslides, subsidence, windstorms, water stress, droughts and rainfall variation at institution/portfolio-level granularity (ECB, n.d.). The source is accessed through a statistics dashboard, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that the underlying supervisory data (AnaCredit/RIAD) is not accessible to an SNCI. In particular, the published output is aggregate/dashboard statistics with no per-exposure data. Consequently, the source cannot be used directly to classify individual exposures, unless the bank replicates the documented methodology using its own AnaCredit-equivalent data plus JRC/Copernicus hazard layers.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is a transparent, replicable methodology covering nine physical hazards with an authoritative EU-level pedigree (ECB, n.d.). It is particularly useful as a methodological template for building an in-house classification approach. However, its suitability is reduced by the inaccessibility of the ECB's own underlying supervisory data to a non-significant institution. It is therefore best used as a methodological anchor rather than as a direct operational data source.

Not applicable via this source directly, since its output is aggregate/dashboard statistics rather than per-exposure data (ECB, n.d.). A per-exposure pipeline would instead need to replicate the ECB's published methodology using the bank's own AnaCredit-equivalent data plus JRC/Copernicus hazard layers.

The source is available under the ECB's standard open-data terms, free of charge and without registration (ECB, n.d.). No restrictions on commercial or systematic use beyond standard attribution practice were identified.

This is a national flood extent dataset, published via the INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, with the Bundesministerium fuer Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Klima- und Umweltschutz, Regionen und Wasserwirtschaft (BMLUK) as data owner and Umweltbundesamt GmbH as technical operator (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-b). It provides harmonised flood extent layers for the 30-, 100- and 300-year return periods, covering flood hazard at parcel/address-level granularity across Austria. The source is accessed through OGC WMS/WFS services and direct GML/shapefile download, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is data currency. In particular, the underlying data has a Datenstand of October 2020, roughly six years old as of this review, and is a composite of several underlying sources (ABU, HORA, BWV/WLV Gefahrenzonenplaene) with potentially inconsistent vintages. Consequently, the source cannot be assumed to reflect flood-protection works or land-use changes made since 2020, unless cross-checked against more recent local information.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable. Its main advantage is combining several underlying Austrian flood sources into a single, harmonised layer with a standard OGC interface and no access restriction, unlike HORA (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-b). It is particularly useful as the primary operational flood layer for populating data point 0050. However, its suitability is reduced somewhat by the dataset's data currency. It is therefore best used as the primary flood-hazard source, complemented by periodic currency checks.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then query the WFS endpoint (nz-core:HazardArea) with each coordinate, or download the GML/shapefile once and perform a local spatial join, assigning the returned flood-zone value to each exposure. The result is parcel/address-level. The process is fully automatable.

The source is available under a CC BY 4.0 licence (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-b). Attribution is required when the data is reused. The licence permits commercial use and systematic portfolio processing.

The Gefahrenzonenplan (GZP) is a public national hazard zoning dataset operated by the Forsttechnischer Dienst fuer Wildbach- und Lawinenverbauung (Federal Ministry BMLUK) (data.gv.at, n.d.-b). It provides a statutory hazard assessment for torrents, avalanches and mass-movement processes, covering these hazards at parcel/address-level granularity across Austria. The source is accessed through an OGC map service (WMS/WFS) and direct download, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that hazards are mapped only within areas of spatial relevance, meaning settled parts of a municipality with designated torrent or avalanche catchments (data.gv.at, n.d.-b). In particular, some zone plans remain available only in analogue form, and a portfolio location without a mapped result is ambiguous - it may indicate no hazard or simply no mapping. Consequently, the source cannot be used to conclusively rule out hazard for unmapped locations, unless cross-checked against the underlying zone-plan status.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable. Its main advantage is being the strongest national source for mass-movement and torrent hazards, based on a statutory hazard assessment under the Forstgesetz (data.gv.at, n.d.-b). It is particularly useful for classifying torrent, avalanche and related mass-movement exposure at data point 0050. However, its suitability is reduced by incomplete settlement-area-only mapping and residual analogue-only zone plans. It is therefore best used as the primary source for these hazards, with unmapped locations flagged for manual review.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then query the WMS/WFS endpoint (data.gv.at, n.d.-b) or download the shapefile/GeoPackage once and perform a local spatial join, assigning the returned zone value to each exposure. The result is parcel/address-level. The process is fully automatable.

The source is available as a High Value Dataset under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138, free of charge with bulk download permitted via the WLV download service in ESRI shapefile format. The licence permits commercial use and systematic portfolio processing.

HORA (Natural Hazard Overview and Risk Assessment Austria) is a publicly accessible Austrian WebGIS application, operated by the Land-, Forst- und Wasserwirtschaftliche Rechenzentrum (LFRZ) on behalf of the responsible federal ministry (LFRZ, n.d.). It provides address- and cadastral-level initial information on natural hazards, currently covering flood, earthquake, storm, hail and snow, at parcel/address-level granularity across Austria (HORA, n.d.). The source is accessed through an interactive web interface via individual location queries, and is free to use.

The main limitation is the restricted use of the service for systematic portfolio-level analysis (LFRZ, n.d.). In particular, the source is designed primarily for individual location queries and does not provide unrestricted bulk download or a documented portfolio-level API, and the displayed information is intended as initial risk information rather than a legally binding assessment. Consequently, HORA cannot be used as the sole source for automated classification of an entire loan portfolio, unless a separate access agreement is obtained from the operator.

For an SNCI, HORA is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is Austrian address-level coverage combined with simple web-based access (HORA, n.d.). It is particularly useful for individual exposure checks and plausibility assessments. However, its suitability is reduced by the restricted portfolio-level access and the non-binding nature of the displayed information. It is therefore best used as a supplementary validation source rather than as the sole operational source for populating data point 0050.

To apply HORA to a portfolio, the institution would need to geocode the relevant exposure addresses and query the corresponding locations individually through the web interface (HORA, n.d.), then record and link the resulting hazard information to each exposure. Because unrestricted bulk access and a documented portfolio-level API are not available, the process is not fully automatable and is unsuitable for systematic portfolio processing under current access conditions.

The source is subject to specific terms of use that restrict bulk download and automated access (LFRZ, n.d.); the service is intended for individual location queries only. A separate agreement with the operator would be required for systematic portfolio-level use or regulatory reporting purposes.

The Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas is a public water-risk dataset operated by the World Resources Institute (WRI) (WRI, n.d.). It provides 13 modelled indicators covering water stress, drought risk and riverine/coastal flood risk at sub-catchment (watershed) granularity globally (WRI, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through a web map portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is coarse granularity relative to Austria's parcel-level sources. In particular, the source resolves only to sub-catchment (watershed) level, so exposures within the same watershed share an identical value, and it is a global tool not locally calibrated or validated for Austria specifically. Consequently, the source cannot differentiate exposures within a geographically concentrated Austrian portfolio, unless combined with finer national sources for the acute hazards it also covers.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is providing dedicated, named indicators for chronic water-related hazards (water stress, drought) otherwise underrepresented among Austrian sources. It is particularly useful as a supplementary chronic-risk layer. However, its suitability is reduced by watershed-level granularity, coarser than the parcel-level Austrian sources for acute hazards. It is therefore best used as a supplementary source for water stress and drought, not as a primary classification layer.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then download the watershed-level dataset or query the API and perform a spatial join to the relevant watershed polygon, assigning the watershed's indicator value to each exposure. The result is sub-catchment (watershed) level. The process is fully automatable.

The source is described by the operator as free and openly accessible for any application, with attribution requested (WRI, n.d.). No formally stated open licence name was identified on the operator's own materials, and no commercial-use restriction was found.

This is a commercial dataset operated by Moody's ESG Solutions (Moody's, n.d.). It provides proprietary modelled physical climate risk scores covering floods, heat stress, hurricanes and typhoons, sea-level rise, water stress and wildfires at facility/object-level granularity globally (Moody's, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through a commercial analytics platform and an API, and is paid.

The main limitation is that confirmed Austria-relevant coverage is narrower than the product's general marketing suggests (Moody's, n.d.-b). In particular, storm is modelled as tropical cyclones specifically, which does not affect Austria, and a distinct heat-wave product plus drought coverage could not be confirmed at all. Consequently, the source cannot be relied upon for storm, heat-wave or drought classification of Austrian exposures, unless the operator confirms specific coverage directly.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is ready-made, high-granularity facility-level risk scores integrable via API with low processing effort (Moody's, n.d.). It is particularly useful for flood, heat stress, water stress and wildfire classification. However, its suitability is reduced by a commercial cost structure typically designed for larger institutions and by narrower-than-marketed Austria-relevant hazard coverage. It is therefore best used as a primary source only for the confirmed hazards, subject to cost negotiation appropriate to SNCI scale.

Pricing is not publicly disclosed. Access is provided through a commercial analytics platform and API under a quote-based licence agreement (Moody's, n.d.). No product-specific price indication was identified; publicly available estimates for other Moody's products should therefore not be used as a proxy. The price information should be treated as not independently verified.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution would send exposure coordinates or addresses to the API (Moody's, n.d.) and receive a facility-level risk score directly. No further spatial processing is required. The process is fully automatable for institutions with API access.

The source is subject to a commercial licence agreement (Moody's, n.d.). Access terms, API scope and portfolio size limits depend on the specific subscription negotiated with Moody's. The licence terms should be reviewed specifically for D 01.01 reporting use cases.

NATHAN Risk Suite is a commercial dataset operated by Munich Re (Munich Re, n.d.). It provides proprietary modelled natural hazard and climate scenario scores covering 15 hazards, including river flood, extratropical storm, wildfire and landslide, at facility/object-level granularity globally, with scenarios extending to 2100 (Munich Re, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through a commercial analytics platform and an API, and is paid.

The main limitation is that heat, drought and water stress coverage could not be confirmed by name (Munich Re, n.d.-b). In particular, these hazards are only advertised via a separate, unnamed 'Climate Change Edition' covering '13 climate hazards' without individual naming in the materials reviewed. Consequently, the source cannot be relied upon for heat, drought or water stress classification with the same confidence as its 15 named Natural Hazards Edition hazards, unless the operator confirms specific coverage directly.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable for its confirmed hazards. Its main advantage is very extensive scenario depth (to 2100) and ready-made facility-level scores for 15 explicitly named hazards, including landslide and extratropical storm. It is particularly useful for portfolio-scale exposure scoring via API. However, its suitability is reduced by pricing typically geared towards larger institutions and reinsurers, and by unconfirmed heat/drought/water-stress coverage. It is therefore best used as a primary source for the confirmed hazards, or via the accessible pay-per-location On-Demand option for smaller-scale use.

Pricing follows two distinct access models (Munich Re, n.d.-c). The On-Demand service uses pay-per-location pricing, with publicly displayed prices ranging from approximately EUR 100 to EUR 160 per location depending on package size. Portfolio-scale access through the Natural Hazards Edition or Climate Change Edition is subscription-based and quote-based, with API access available in the relevant business tiers. The publicly displayed On-Demand prices are not directly comparable with portfolio subscription costs.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution would send exposure coordinates or addresses to the API (Munich Re, n.d.) and receive a facility-level risk score directly. No further spatial processing is required. The process is fully automatable for institutions with API/subscription access.

The source is subject to a commercial licence agreement. The On-Demand service requires no subscription and is billed per location; portfolio-scale subscription tiers (Natural Hazards Edition, Climate Change Edition) determine API access and portfolio size limits. The licence terms should be reviewed specifically for D 01.01 reporting use cases.

This is a public dataset collection operated by the World Bank Group in cooperation with GFDRR (World Bank/GFDRR, n.d.), comprising the Risk Data Library (downloadable hazard datasets) and the ThinkHazard! screening tool. It provides flood, landslide, wildfire, extreme-heat and water-scarcity hazard information at district (ADM2) to dataset-dependent granularity, with a development-country focus (GFDRR, n.d.). The source is accessed through a web portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is granularity that is not uniform across the source. In particular, ThinkHazard! resolves only to district (ADM2) level, while Risk Data Library datasets vary individually in resolution, and storm coverage via ThinkHazard!'s 'cyclone' hazard model is tropical-cyclone-oriented with unconfirmed applicability to Austria. Consequently, the source cannot differentiate exposures within a single Austrian district, unless combined with finer national sources.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is confirmed, commonly-available probabilistic coverage for flood, landslide, extreme heat, water scarcity and wildfire, accessible free via API (GFDRR, n.d.). It is particularly useful for plausibility checks and district-level screening. However, its suitability is reduced by district-level, not parcel-level, granularity. It is therefore best used as a supplementary or validation source rather than as the primary operational layer.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then determine the ADM2 (district) administrative unit for each coordinate and query the ThinkHazard! API for the hazard level of that district, or download the relevant Risk Data Library dataset for gridded hazards and perform a spatial join, assigning the resulting value to each exposure. The result is district-level. The process is fully automatable, though district-level resolution limits differentiation.

The source is available under the World Bank's open-data terms, free of charge and without registration (World Bank/GFDRR, n.d.). No restrictions on commercial or systematic use beyond standard attribution practice were identified.

KryoMon.AT is a publicly funded research consortium coordinated by the University of Graz, involving multiple Austrian universities, the Austrian and Bavarian Academies of Sciences, GeoSphere Austria and several associations (KryoMon.AT, n.d.; ORF Steiermark, 2026). It provides periodic reports on permafrost, glacier and snow trends covering permafrost hazard at station-based granularity across selected Austrian alpine sites (KryoMon.AT, n.d.). The source is accessed through a reports/publications website with PDF downloads, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that the information exists only as narrative PDF reports, not as structured per-location data (KryoMon.AT, n.d.). In particular, coverage is station-/object-based rather than a nationwide spatial hazard layer. Consequently, the source cannot be overlaid with individual portfolio locations, unless the bank undertakes manual, qualitative interpretation per region.

For an SNCI, the source is not suitable for systematic classification. Its main advantage is being the best available current context on Austrian permafrost trends, produced by an authoritative multi-institutional research consortium (KryoMon.AT, n.d.; ORF Steiermark, 2026). It is particularly useful for background discussion and methodological context in the reporting narrative. However, its suitability is reduced by the complete absence of structured, location-specific data. It is therefore best used purely as a context source, not as an operational data source.

Not applicable: the information exists only in narrative PDF reports (KryoMon.AT, n.d.), not as structured per-location data, so no automatable pipeline can be built against it. At best, a qualitative note per region could be manually derived.

The source is available under the reporting consortium's general open-access publication terms, free of charge, with attribution expected per standard academic practice (KryoMon.AT, n.d.). No commercial-use restriction was identified.

This is a public register operated by Statistik Austria (Statistik Austria, n.d.). It provides the official OeNACE 2025 (NACE Rev. 2.1) economic-activity code for each Austrian company, keyed to the Firmenbuch number, covering the full national company register at entity-level granularity. The source is accessed through direct bulk download in CSV format, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is incomplete company coverage (Statistik Austria, n.d.). In particular, companies without an assigned OeNACE code remain unmatched, and unregistered sole traders are out of scope of the Firmenbuch-based register. Consequently, the source cannot classify every possible counterparty in an SNCI's loan portfolio, unless a complementary source is used for the unmatched residual.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable. Its main advantage is being simultaneously official, freely accessible in bulk and directly joinable to a loan portfolio via the Firmenbuchnummer (Statistik Austria, n.d.). It is particularly useful as the primary operational source for populating the NACE subsector dimension. However, its suitability is reduced slightly by unmatched companies and out-of-scope sole traders. It is therefore best used as the primary transition-risk classification source, complemented by Wirtschafts-Compass where an existing licence is operationally simpler.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution can bulk-download the CSV file (Statistik Austria, n.d.) and join it directly to its internal exposure data using the Firmenbuchnummer, then transform the assigned OeNACE code to the required 4-digit reporting granularity. The result is entity-level. The process is fully automatable and does not require geocoding or spatial processing.

The source is available under a CC BY 4.0 licence, published as a High Value Dataset under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138. Attribution is required when the data is reused. The licence permits commercial use and systematic portfolio processing.

Wirtschafts-Compass is a commercial Austrian company-data service operated by Compass-Verlag GmbH (Compass-Verlag, n.d.). It provides an editorially enriched OeNACE classification per entity, covering the Austrian company landscape at entity-level granularity, delivered with daily currency. The source is accessed through an API and a web portal, and is paid.

The main limitation is that the classification is editorially enriched rather than the official statistical assignment (Compass-Verlag, n.d.). In particular, cost is institution-dependent, since some banks may already hold a sector licence while others would face a new subscription cost. Consequently, the source cannot be treated as an authoritative regulatory reference on the same footing as the official HVD dataset, unless used alongside HVD for cross-validation.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable. Its main advantage is being directly usable, daily-updated and API-accessible, with existing institutional access reported in parts of the Austrian banking sector (Compass-Verlag, n.d.-b). It is particularly useful where an existing licence makes a single query operationally simpler than a bulk HVD join. However, its suitability is reduced by cost for institutions without an existing licence and by its non-official classification status. It is therefore best used as a primary operational source alongside the free HVD dataset.

Pricing is publicly disclosed for standard access: pay-per-query, from EUR 6 (excl. VAT) per quarter for up to 10 queries via the WKO-member service, or from EUR 24 per year for individual/basic access (Compass-Verlag, n.d.-c; Compass-Verlag, n.d.-d). Institutional/enterprise API pricing is not publicly listed and should be confirmed directly with the provider.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution would send the Firmenbuchnummer or company identifier to the API (Compass-Verlag, n.d.) and receive the OeNACE classification directly. No further processing is required. The process is fully automatable for institutions with API access.

The source is subject to a commercial licence agreement (Compass-Verlag, n.d.-c). Standard access is pay-per-query with published pricing; institutional API access terms depend on the specific subscription. The licence terms should be reviewed specifically for D 01.01 reporting use cases.

SPARTACUS-v3 is a public gridded climate dataset operated by GeoSphere Austria, the Austrian federal institute for geology, geophysics, climatology and meteorology (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). It provides observed daily, monthly and quarterly temperature, precipitation and sunshine-duration fields, covering heat and precipitation hazards at 1km grid granularity across Austria since 1961 (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). The source is accessed through a web interface, a coordinate-based REST API and HTTP bulk download, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that the source provides raw climate variables, not a pre-classified hazard or risk score (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). In particular, converting temperature or precipitation fields into a heat-wave or heavy-precipitation exposure indicator requires the institution's own threshold definition. Consequently, the source cannot be used directly for exposure classification, unless the bank first defines and validates its own index methodology.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable. Its main advantage is Austria's highest-resolution national gridded observation dataset, finer than Copernicus CDS, with a coordinate-based API enabling direct point queries (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). It is particularly useful as the primary raw-data foundation for heat and heavy-precipitation indices tailored to Austrian conditions. However, its suitability is reduced by the own-methodology effort required to convert raw variables into a hazard indicator. It is therefore best used as a primary source for institutions willing to define their own threshold-based indices.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then query the GeoSphere Austria grid API with the coordinates for the relevant variable and apply a chosen threshold definition, assigning the resulting indicator to each exposure. The result is grid-level (1km). The process is fully automatable once the threshold methodology is defined.

The source is available under the Creative Commons Public Domain Dedication (CC0 1.0), per GeoSphere Austria's own repository documentation, free for any use including commercial. No attribution is legally required, though it is good practice. The licence permits systematic portfolio processing.

WINFORE is a public gridded drought-index dataset operated by GeoSphere Austria (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-b). It provides the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) at 30-, 90- and 365-day aggregation, covering drought hazard at 1km grid granularity across Austria, derived from SPARTACUS temperature and precipitation fields. The source is accessed through a web interface, a coordinate-based REST API and HTTP bulk download, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that SPEI is a standardised statistical anomaly index, not an absolute water-deficit value (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-b). In particular, it is derived via a normal-distribution transform over two climate reference periods, so its interpretation requires understanding this transform rather than reading a direct precipitation deficit. Consequently, the source cannot be interpreted at face value without methodological context, unless the reporting institution documents the SPEI transform in its own methodology notes.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable. Its main advantage is being a dedicated, purpose-built national drought index at fine (1km) resolution, filling a gap not covered by any other Austrian source in this matrix. It is particularly useful as the primary drought-classification source for data point 0050. However, its suitability is reduced somewhat by the need to correctly interpret the standardised anomaly value. It is therefore best used as the primary drought source, with a brief methodology note on SPEI interpretation.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then query the GeoSphere Austria grid API with the coordinates for the WINFORE SPEI variable at the desired aggregation window, assigning the returned value to each exposure. The result is grid-level (1km). The process is fully automatable.

The source is available under the Creative Commons Public Domain Dedication (CC0 1.0), per GeoSphere Austria's own repository documentation, free for any use including commercial. No attribution is legally required, though it is good practice.

Spectra is a commercial physical climate risk platform operated by Climate X Ltd, a UK-based company founded in 2020 (Technology Tools, n.d.). It provides asset-level modelled physical hazard scores and financial loss projections across up to 16 hazards, including flooding, storms, heat stress, wildfires and landslides, at asset/facility-level granularity globally, with scenario projections to 2100 (Repath, n.d.). The source is accessed through a commercial SaaS platform and an API, and is paid.

The main limitation is that pricing and the full hazard list are not published by the operator directly (Net Zero Compare, n.d.). In particular, only third-party estimates of cost are available, not operator-confirmed figures. Consequently, the source's exact scope and cost cannot be independently verified from public information, unless confirmed directly with Climate X.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is ready-made, high-granularity asset-level scores integrable via API for a broad set of confirmed hazards (Repath, n.d.; Net Zero Compare, n.d.). It is particularly useful for flood, storm, heat stress, wildfire and landslide classification. However, its suitability is reduced by unconfirmed pricing and enterprise-SaaS positioning that may exceed a typical SNCI's budget. It is therefore best used as a primary source subject to direct price confirmation appropriate to SNCI scale.

Pricing is not publicly disclosed by Climate X directly. Access is provided through a commercial SaaS platform and API under a quote-based licence agreement. Third-party industry comparison sources estimate EUR 20,000-60,000 per year for portfolios of 30-100 assets, described as 'mid-market' pricing (Repath, n.d.). The price information should be treated as indicative and not independently verified.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution would send exposure coordinates or addresses to the Spectra API (Climate X, n.d.) and receive an asset-level hazard/financial-loss score directly. No further spatial processing is required. The process is fully automatable for institutions with API access.

The source is subject to a commercial licence agreement, quote-based, with no public price list (Net Zero Compare, n.d.). Access terms and portfolio size limits depend on the specific subscription negotiated. The licence terms should be reviewed specifically for D 01.01 reporting use cases.

ClimateScore Global is a commercial physical climate risk platform operated by Jupiter Intelligence, Inc., a US company founded in 2017 (aigreentools.com, n.d.). It provides asset-level modelled physical hazard scores and finance-grade loss metrics across 9 physical perils, including flood, heat, drought, tropical cyclones and wildfire, at asset/facility-level granularity globally, based on peer-reviewed CMIP6/ERA5 science (aigreentools.com, n.d.). The source is accessed through a commercial SaaS platform and an API, and is paid.

The main limitation is enterprise-tier, quote-based pricing not publicly listed (Mitiga Solutions, n.d.). In particular, the platform's scientific and financial-metric depth is designed for enterprise-scale deployments across banks, insurers and asset managers. Consequently, the source cannot be assumed affordable for an SNCI without direct confirmation, unless a limited-scope engagement at the lower end of the stated price range is negotiated.

For an SNCI, the source is conditionally suitable. Its main advantage is extensive, scientifically validated hazard and financial-metric coverage across 9 peer-reviewed perils (aigreentools.com, n.d.). It is particularly useful for institutions needing finance-grade physical risk metrics beyond simple hazard scores. However, its suitability is reduced by enterprise-tier pricing likely above a typical SNCI's budget for full portfolio deployment. It is therefore best used as a primary source for a limited scope, subject to direct price negotiation.

Pricing is not publicly disclosed as a fixed list, but is quote-based. Jupiter's own CEO stated in a 2022 interview that 'subscription pricing ranges from $25,000 to multimillion-dollar contracts' depending on scope (Trellis/Clancy, 2022). Full portfolio deployments are typically six-figure annual commitments per third-party sources (Repath, n.d.). The price information should be treated as indicative, based on the operator's own public statement.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution would send exposure coordinates or addresses to the ClimateScore Global API (Jupiter Intelligence, n.d.) and receive an asset-level hazard/financial-loss score directly. No further spatial processing is required. The process is fully automatable for institutions with API access.

The source is subject to a commercial licence agreement, quote-based and defined case-by-case with the client (Mitiga Solutions, n.d.). Access terms and portfolio size limits depend on the specific subscription negotiated. The licence terms should be reviewed specifically for D 01.01 reporting use cases.

This is a set of standalone, ready-made physical hazard indicator products, published as individual datasets on the Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS), distinct from the general-purpose raw climate variables covered by the separate copernicus_cds entry (ECMWF, n.d.). It provides ERA5-HEAT (UTCI/heat stress) and the SMHI hydrology dataset (flood, water stress/aridity, soil-moisture drought), covering these four hazards at grid granularity across Europe (Di Napoli et al., 2021; SMHI/C3S, n.d.). The source is accessed through direct download and a queryable API, and is free of charge.

The main limitation is that meteorological (SPI-3) drought and the temperature/precipitation/wind-based ECDE indices (heat wave, heavy precipitation, storm) remain accessible only via raw copernicus_cds variables or the Climate-ADAPT-curated bundle, not as a standalone product under this entry. Consequently, a bank needing those specific indices cannot rely on this entry alone, unless it also consults copernicus_cds or eea_climate_adapt for them.

For an SNCI, the source is suitable. Its main advantage is that each product is a purpose-built, documented hazard indicator with no own index-definition effort required, unlike raw Copernicus CDS variables (Di Napoli et al., 2021; SMHI/C3S, n.d.). It is particularly useful for heat stress, flood, water stress and soil-moisture drought classification at low processing effort. However, its suitability is reduced by its narrower hazard breadth compared with the full CDS catalogue. It is therefore best used as a primary source for its four covered hazards, complemented by other sources for the remainder.

To apply the source to a portfolio, the institution must first geocode the relevant exposure addresses to coordinates. It must then query or download the relevant standalone product (ERA5-HEAT for heat stress, SMHI hydrology for flood/water stress/soil-moisture drought) for the coordinate, assigning the returned value to each exposure. The result is grid-level. The process is fully automatable.

The source is available under CC-BY 4.0 since 2 July 2025, the same licence as copernicus_cds (ECMWF Forum, 2025), replacing the prior "Licence to Use Copernicus Products" (Version 1.2, Nov 2019). Attribution is required when the data is reused. The licence permits commercial use and systematic portfolio processing.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source is accessed through a statistics dashboard with no download or API. The rating reflects only the effort to access and read the source's own aggregate output; it does not include the substantially higher, distinct effort of replicating a similar analysis using the institution's own portfolio data, since the EBA ESG Dashboard provides no per-exposure data at all.

Technical effort is rated High because the source provides no bulk download or API, only individual web-interface queries. Each portfolio location must be manually looked up and the resulting hazard information manually recorded and linked back to the exposure, since no structured, machine-readable output exists for systematic processing.

Technical effort is rated Medium because the source provides pre-computed, named indicators (e.g. baseline water stress, riverine flood risk) directly via API or download, so no own index definition is needed. However, geocoding of exposure addresses and a spatial join to the relevant watershed (Pfafstetter basin) polygon are still required before a value can be assigned to an exposure.

Technical effort is rated Medium because the ThinkHazard! component provides a pre-computed, categorical hazard level directly via API once the ADM2 (district) unit is determined, requiring geocoding but no own index definition. However, the Risk Data Library component provides gridded/vector datasets of varying formats that require their own spatial overlay, so overall effort is higher than for a single ready-made API product.

Technical effort is rated High because the source exists only as narrative PDF reports, not as structured, machine-readable per-location data. There is no download format, API or spatial layer to query; any use requires manual reading and qualitative interpretation of the reports, with no possibility of an automated pipeline.

Technical effort is rated Medium because the source provides gridded 1km daily climate data (temperature, precipitation, sunshine) via a coordinate-based API. While the raw variables are directly queryable without geocoding difficulty, the institution must define its own hazard thresholds (for example, a heat-wave or heavy-precipitation definition) to convert the climate data into a regulatory-relevant indicator. This climatological processing step distinguishes it from sources with pre-defined hazard indices.

Technical effort is rated Medium because the source provides a gridded 1km drought index (SPEI) via a coordinate-based API, so unlike raw climate variables no own drought-index computation is needed. However, geocoding of exposure addresses and correct interpretation of the standardised SPEI anomaly value (rather than reading it as an absolute deficit) are still required before assigning a classification to an exposure.

Technical effort is rated Low because the source provides ready-made asset-level hazard and financial-loss scores, directly integrable via API. No own index definition, geocoding or spatial processing is required beyond sending exposure coordinates or addresses to the API, consistent with the Low rating for other commercial facility/asset-level providers (Moody's, Munich Re).

Technical effort is rated Low because the source provides ready-made asset-level hazard and finance-grade loss scores, directly integrable via API. No own index definition, geocoding or spatial processing is required beyond sending exposure coordinates or addresses to the API, consistent with the Low rating for other commercial facility/asset-level providers.

The source is based on the ECDE indicator set, computed by the Climate Data Factory and B-Open under a C3S service contract from established EURO-CORDEX/ERA5 climate projections, with each index individually documented and traceable to named peer-reviewed methodology papers (e.g. Spinoni et al., 2018/2020; Jacob et al., 2013). Known issues: the EEA's own summary report table resolves only to European macro-regions, while the underlying indicator dataset itself is considerably finer; resolution varies by indicator from 5km to approximately 28km (EEA/C3S, n.d.).

The source is based on modelled hazard, exposure and historical-loss data compiled by the Joint Research Centre from multiple national and EU inputs, documented in JRC technical reports (Antofie et al., 2023). Known issues: the Vulnerability and Risk Analysis modules are explicitly described by JRC itself as 'ongoing work'; only the Exposure Analysis and Historical Events modules are reliably documented and hazard-verified at present.

The source is based primarily on ERA5 reanalysis and EURO-CORDEX climate projections, produced by ECMWF and national contributing centres under C3S and documented through peer-reviewed literature and individual CDS catalogue entries (ECMWF, n.d.). Known issues: quality, vintage and resolution vary considerably across the more than 140 datasets hosted on the CDS, so no single quality statement applies uniformly - each dataset must be assessed on its own documentation.

The source is based on aggregated supervisory data compiled by the European Banking Authority from EU/EEA banks' regulatory reporting, with the underlying methodology documented in the EBA's risk dashboard technical notes (EBA, n.d.-a). Known issues: aggregation to EU bank-level obscures any institution- or exposure-level variation entirely, since the dashboard was not designed for granular or per-exposure use.

The source is based on ECB-compiled indicators combining AnaCredit/RIAD supervisory data with JRC/Copernicus hazard layers, with the methodology published and updated across successive numbered releases (ECB, n.d.). Known issues: heat stress inclusion is inconsistent across the ECB's own communications - named in some contexts but absent from the core 9-hazard indicator list - which is flagged here as a documentation inconsistency pending clarification.

The source is based on a composite of Abflussuntersuchungen (ABU), HORA and BWV/WLV hazard-zoning inputs, published via the INSPIRE Geoportal with BMLUK as data owner (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-b). Known issues: the Datenstand is October 2020, roughly six years old as of this review, and the underlying component datasets may carry inconsistent vintages, since they are separately maintained and merged into a single layer.

The source is based on a compilation of multiple underlying Austrian hazard datasets (flood, earthquake, storm, hail, snow), presented by the operator explicitly as initial screening information rather than a validated legal assessment (LFRZ, n.d.). Known issues: the operator itself states that the map content is not legally binding, and the vintage of the individual underlying hazard layers per query is not disclosed to the user.

The source is based on the Aqueduct 4.0 modelled water-risk framework, produced by the World Resources Institute using global hydrological models with a publicly documented methodology (WRI, n.d.-b). Known issues: as a global model, it is not locally calibrated or independently validated specifically for Austria, and watershed-level aggregation may obscure local variation within a single sub-catchment.

The source is based on proprietary modelled physical risk scores, originally developed by Four Twenty Seven, Inc. and now operated by Moody's ESG Solutions following the 2019 acquisition (Moody's, n.d.-b). Known issues: the underlying methodology is not fully transparent or independently validated, as is typical for proprietary commercial risk models, and confirmed Austria-relevant hazard coverage is narrower than the product's general marketing suggests.

The source is based on proprietary modelled natural hazard and climate scenario scores, produced by Munich Re, a reinsurer with decades of natural-catastrophe modelling experience (Munich Re, n.d.-b). Known issues: the underlying methodology is not fully public and independent third-party validation is limited; only the 15 explicitly named Natural Hazards Edition hazards are confirmed, while heat, drought and water-stress coverage under the separate 'Climate Change Edition' could not be individually verified.

The source is based on periodic reports from a multi-institutional Austrian research consortium coordinated by the University of Graz, involving multiple universities and the Austrian and Bavarian Academies of Sciences (KryoMon.AT, n.d.). Known issues: reporting is narrative and qualitative rather than following a fixed statistical methodology, published irregularly with no disclosed fixed schedule, and no structured, machine-readable per-location data exists.

The source is based on editorially compiled and enriched company data, produced by Compass-Verlag GmbH, a long-established Austrian commercial business-information provider (Compass-Verlag, n.d.). Known issues: as an editorial rather than official classification, its methodology is not independently published or peer-reviewed, and individual entries may diverge from the official Statistik Austria HVD assignment - cross-validation against HVD is advisable where feasible.

The source is based on gridded observational climate data produced by GeoSphere Austria from station measurements interpolated to a 1km grid, with the methodology documented in peer-reviewed literature and in operational use since 1961 (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). Known issues: the interpolation process introduces some uncertainty in data-sparse high-alpine regions, and the most recent seven days of data are provisional pending final quality control.

The source is based on the SPEI drought index, derived from SPARTACUS temperature and precipitation fields using an established statistical methodology (a normal-distribution transform over defined climate reference periods), standard in the international drought-monitoring literature (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-b). Known issues: as a standardised anomaly index, SPEI requires correct interpretation relative to its reference period rather than being read as an absolute water deficit.

The source is based on proprietary modelled asset-level physical risk scores, produced by Climate X Ltd, a UK-based climate-risk analytics company founded in 2020 (Technology Tools, n.d.). Known issues: neither the full methodology nor the complete hazard list is published by the operator directly, and no independent third-party validation was identified; pricing and hazard-list completeness rely on third-party industry sources rather than operator confirmation.

The source is based on proprietary modelled asset-level physical risk and financial-loss metrics, produced by Jupiter Intelligence, Inc. from peer-reviewed CMIP6/ERA5 climate science (aigreentools.com, n.d.). Known issues: while the underlying climate science is peer-reviewed and publicly documented, the proprietary loss-translation methodology is not independently validated, and the only available pricing indication is a single CEO interview statement rather than a published price list.

The source comprises two named, quality-controlled products: ERA5-HEAT, peer-reviewed and produced by ECMWF (Di Napoli et al., 2021), and the SMHI hydrology dataset, produced and quality-assured by the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute for C3S (SMHI/C3S, n.d.). Known issues: the SMHI hydrology projections are static 30-year model outputs rather than continuously updated, so their currency should be checked against the stated reference period before use.
